name: CHOLMOD (SuiteSparse supernodal sparse Cholesky, via Eigen::CholmodSupernodalLLT)
baseline: Eigen::SimplicialLLT and Eigen::SimplicialLDLT (Eigen's built-in sparse Cholesky); Eigen::SparseLU also in the table
workload: Factorization time of SPD k-harmonic diffusion systems (k=1,2,3) on the 720K-vertex xyzrgb_dragon triangle mesh, Eigen wrappers around each solver.
claimed_speedup: Factor time vs Eigen::SimplicialLLT: 0.86 s vs 1.5 s for harmonic (about 1.7x, derived from page data), 1.7 s vs 12 s for biharmonic (about 7x, derived), 3.3 s vs 41 s for triharmonic (about 12x, derived); Eigen::SparseLU needed 4.8 s, 31 s and 130 s. Solve phase only about 1.2x to 1.4x better (0.1 s vs 0.12 s harmonic).
hardware: MacBook, 2.3 GHz quad-core Intel Core i7, 32 GB RAM
license: GPL-2.0-or-later (CHOLMOD Supernodal module); LGPL-2.1-or-later for CHOLMOD's other modules
tradeoffs: Supernodal module is GPL; needs BLAS/LAPACK; the Eigen wrapper adds a SuiteSparse dependency; factorization only for SPD matrices (LDL^T variant also exists).
caveats: CHOLMOD is itself the incumbent for this category (SuiteSparse), so this entry records it as the shootout winner over Eigen's own simplicial solvers rather than as a new library. Informal single-author benchmark: one mesh, one laptop, compiler not stated, README says 'YMMV'. Errors differ slightly across solvers (L-infinity 1e-10 to 1e-4 depending on k). Eigen::PardisoLLT also beats Eigen simplicial on k=2 and k=3 but is proprietary; catamari::SparseLDL (MPL-2.0) was not faster than Eigen simplicial. Per-module licences were not opened beyond the SuiteSparse page note that some modules are GPL.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'sparse Cholesky LDL library faster than CHOLMOD Eigen benchmark github' surfaced alecjacobson/sparse-solver-benchmark; README opened via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: SPC5 (block-based SpMV kernels for AVX-512 and ARM SVE)
baseline: Intel MKL CSR SpMV (sequential column of the results CSV)
workload: Sequential SpMV y=Ax over 23 SuiteSparse matrices in double and float on AVX-512, SPC5 kernels 1rVc/2rVc/4rVc/8rVc compared with MKL CSR, in GFlop/s.
claimed_speedup: From results/results-avx-2.csv, taking the best of the four SPC5 sequential kernels per matrix against the MKL column (derived from page data): median 1.23x in double and 1.49x in float, geometric mean 1.18x and 1.45x, SPC5 ahead on 16 of 23 matrices in double and 17 of 23 in float, up to 1.90x (double) and 3.00x (float), but slower on others (worst 0.45x double, 0.41x float).
compiler_and_flags: g++ 11.2.0 with MKL 2022.0.2 (from jobs-plafrim.sh); CMake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=RELEASE -DUSE_AVX512=ON -DCPU=CNL; OpenMP with OMP_PROC_BIND=true
hardware: PlaFRIM 'bora' Intel Cascade Lake nodes (SLURM constraint bora&intel&cascadelake, 36 CPUs per task); exact CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Needs a conversion from CSR to SPC5's block formats; AVX-512 or ARM SVE only (SVE emulated on x86 through FARM); C++17; compact code meant to be copied (spc5.hpp).
caveats: The best kernel is picked per matrix after the fact, which flatters SPC5; the CSV has an MKL column only for sequential runs (parallel SPC5 columns have no MKL counterpart). Conversion cost is not examined in the numbers I read. Results are a 2023 re-run, not the numbers of the 2018 PeerJ CS paper (paper page could not be opened, peerj.com is blocked here). CPU class only, no model.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'SpMV library CPU AVX-512 outperforms Intel MKL sparse BLAS github open source' surfaced berenger-eu/spc5; README, jobs-plafrim.sh and results CSV opened via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: CKTSO (parallel sparse direct solver for circuit simulation)
language: C (prebuilt shared libraries with a C header; source not published)
baseline: KLU from SuiteSparse (sequential, approximate minimum degree ordering); README also names NICSLU, Intel MKL PARDISO and two GPU-based sparse solvers
workload: LU factorization and solve of 66 circuit matrices from the SuiteSparse collection (dimensions 1K to 5M).
claimed_speedup: README: on average more than 3X faster than KLU when sequential and more than 25X faster with 16 threads; on average faster than KLU, NICSLU, Intel MKL PARDISO and two GPU solvers for circuit matrices (detailed tables are in doc/results.pdf, not opened).
tradeoffs: x86-64 binaries only (CentOS 6/7, Rocky 8, Windows 7 x64); needs a license key file (license/cktso.lic) next to the library; specialised for SPICE-style circuit matrices; races 10 reordering methods, so analysis is slow by design.
caveats: Repository ships compiled libraries, a header, demos and docs, not source, and the licence is a key file whose terms were not visible, so it is not OSI-open and cannot be audited. Averages are first-party and the per-matrix PDF (a 2022 version, 'results are from an old version') was not opened. The IEEE TCAD 2025 paper cited in the README was not opened. Hardware, compiler and thread-count setup are not given on the README.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'sparse LU circuit simulation solver "faster than KLU" github' surfaced chenxm1986/cktso; README opened via raw.githubusercontent.com and the repo page via WebFetch

name: GraphBLAST (GraphBLAS on the GPU)
workload: BFS, SSSP, PageRank and triangle counting on 10 to 13 SuiteSparse/SNAP/LAW graphs, GraphBLAST on a GTX 1070 against LAGraph on the host CPU, as drawn by the competing spla project.
claimed_speedup: Read by eye from the log-scale speedup-over-LAGraph chart in the spla README (approximate, no numeric table): GraphBLAST PageRank roughly 13x to 75x, triangle counting roughly 5x to 13x, BFS roughly 0.4x to 4.5x and SSSP roughly 0.2x to 2.6x (slower than LAGraph on some graphs).
hardware: Intel Core i7-6700 3.40 GHz 4-core, 64 GB DDR4, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1070 8 GB, Ubuntu 20.04
tradeoffs: NVIDIA CUDA only, Boost dependency, tested on CUDA 9.1/9.2 with g++ 4.9.3/5.4.0 per the README, so it may need porting to build on current toolchains.
caveats: The evidence is a third-party chart in another project's README, not GraphBLAST's own page, and the GPU-versus-CPU comparison is not like for like. GraphBLAST's own TOPC paper (arXiv 1908.01407) reportedly claims 43.51x geometric-mean speedup over multi-threaded SuiteSparse GraphBLAS, but I saw that figure only in a search-result summary because arxiv.org is blocked here, so it is unverified. Last commit 2021.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'github GraphBLAS GPU implementation faster than SuiteSparse:GraphBLAS benchmark' surfaced gunrock/graphblast; numbers read from the spla README chart docs/stats/rq1_rel.png

name: PanguLU (distributed heterogeneous sparse LU, regular 2D block-cyclic)
workload: Sparse LU factorization on distributed platforms with up to 128 NVIDIA A100 GPUs and up to 128 AMD MI50 GPUs (SC'23 paper).
claimed_speedup: SC'23 abstract as summarised by a web search: up to 11.70x (A100 cluster) and 17.97x (MI50 cluster) over the latest SuperLU_DIST. Not confirmed on an opened page: the paper hosts (acm.org, sc23.supercomputing.org, researchgate) are blocked in this container and the repo README contains no benchmark.
hardware: 128 NVIDIA A100 or 128 AMD MI50 GPUs per the paper summary
tradeoffs: AGPL-3.0 is strong copyleft; needs MPI, optional CUDA (12.9 tested) and METIS; library written in C with build options set through make.inc and -D flags.
caveats: Peer-reviewed tier is inferred from the SC'23 paper; the numbers are unverified here and are best-case ('up to') figures on large GPU clusters, not single-node results. The repo has since moved to version 5.0.0, so the current code may differ from what the paper measured.

name: LAMG+ (lean algebraic multigrid for graph Laplacians)
baseline: PETSc GAMG; the same study also runs hypre BoomerAMG, pyAMG, CMG and approximate Cholesky (Laplacians.jl approxchol_lap)
workload: Setup plus solve time per nonzero (microseconds/nnz) to relative residual 1e-8 on graph-Laplacian systems from a class-stratified SuiteSparse/SNAP corpus, serial runs, one Julia process.
claimed_speedup: Class table in doc/lamg_plus.tex, mean microseconds/nnz LAMG+ vs PETSc GAMG: social/citation 0.47 vs 3.10 (about 6.6x, derived from page data), web 0.37 vs 2.76 (7.5x), optimization 0.15 vs 2.04 (13.6x), chimera 0.40 vs 0.91, weighted chimera 0.45 vs 0.96, SDDM chimera 0.30 vs 1.74, anisotropic grid 0.61 vs 1.01; tie on FE/structural (0.12 vs 0.12); PETSc GAMG faster on mesh/grid (0.84 vs 0.23), 3D grid (1.30 vs 0.25), roads (0.68 vs 0.57) and SPE reservoir (1.09 vs 0.90). Versus BoomerAMG: social 0.47 vs 1.53, web 0.37 vs 1.43, optimization 0.15 vs 4.07.
compiler_and_flags: Julia 1.10 or newer (notebook kernel julia-1.12); competitors run in the same Julia process; build flags not stated
hardware: Apple M5 Pro, 18 cores, 48 GB RAM
tradeoffs: Graph-Laplacian systems only (SPD with the constant vector in the null space); empirically linear-time but no worst-case guarantee; hierarchy memory is 62 to 80 bytes/nnz on web/social graphs against 32 to 40 for approximate Cholesky, and 22 to 30 bytes/nnz on FE/structural matrices.
caveats: Author-run, first-party; the paper in the repo (doc/lamg_plus.tex) is the evidence. PETSc GAMG is the incumbent only on some classes: it beats LAMG+ on grids, roads and SPE and fails to converge on 6 instances. The strongest peer, approxChol, beats LAMG+ on social/web/road graphs; against it LAMG+ is at parity (0.99x geometric mean over 201 graphs) and wins on FE/structural matrices (for example bmwcra_1 0.08 vs 0.28). Competitors reach PETSc/hypre through Julia wrappers. Commit history shows AI-assistant co-authorship.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'algebraic multigrid solver github "faster than" hypre BoomerAMG OR PETSc GAMG benchmark' surfaced LAMG+; README and doc/lamg_plus.tex opened via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: Sputnik (sparse GPU kernels for deep learning: SpMM and SDDMM)
workload: Sparse-times-dense matrix multiply (SpMM) at M=N=K=64 and M=N=K=4096, densities 0.05 to 0.5, on an A100, timed by the third-party Torch-Sputnik wrapper.
claimed_speedup: M=N=K=4096, time in ms (page states ms): Sputnik 2.52 vs cuSPARSE 10.97 at density 0.05 (about 4.4x, derived from page data), 4.02 vs 21.68 at 0.1 (5.4x), 13.05 vs 107.38 at 0.5 (8.2x). M=N=K=64: Sputnik 0.0045 to 0.0075 vs cuSPARSE 0.086 to 0.147.
hardware: NVIDIA A100 (host CPU, CUDA and compiler versions not stated)
tradeoffs: NVIDIA only (SM70+), CUDA 10.1+, glog dependency, built with CMake; aimed at the sparse matrices of deep neural networks.
caveats: Numbers come from a third-party PyTorch binding repo, not Sputnik's own README (which has none); the SC'20 paper (Gale et al., 'Sparse GPU Kernels for Deep Learning') is the primary evidence but was not opened. The same table shows dense cuBLAS at 7.29 ms for 4096^3, so Sputnik is slower than dense at density 0.5 (13.05 ms) and 0.25 (7.87 ms) and only wins at densities of about 0.2 and below. Repository is archived and has not changed since 2020.

name: RSLAB (pure-Rust sparse LDL^T, LU and KLU solver)
workload: Wall time relative to PARDISO on 28 systems exported from production codes (6 FEM curl-curl, 2 power grid, 7 MoM near field, 13 SuiteSparse circuits), 12 threads each, geometric mean per class.
claimed_speedup: Ratios to PARDISO time (below 1 is faster): solve 0.34 / 0.43 / 0.37 / 0.30 on the four classes (about 2.3x to 3.3x faster, derived from page data); factor 1.35 / 3.97 / 0.95 / 4.76 and refactor 1.38 / 4.28 / 0.90 / 1.83 (faster only on MoM near field); one-shot analysis+factor+solve 1.05 / 1.06 / 0.74 / 1.12 (faster only on MoM near field).
tradeoffs: No BLAS, LAPACK or MKL needed; factor is bit-identical for every thread count; Python bindings (pip install rslab); built-in Krylov solvers use the factor as preconditioner; Threads::Auto is capped at 4 workers by default.
caveats: Mixed result: the win is the solve phase; factorization and one-shot time are slower than PARDISO on three of four classes. The corpus is exported from production codes and the benchmark scripts take a corpus path, so the table cannot be reproduced from the README alone. CPU model, Rust version and flags are not given. MKL PARDISO is a proprietary baseline. The project started from the feral crate (MIT) and its commit history is very recent.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/sparse-linear-solver listing led to milanofthe/rslab; README opened via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: DirectLUSolvers (MultifrontalQR, SupernodalLDLT, LeftRightLU for Eigen)
baseline: Eigen::SparseQR (for MultifrontalQR); Eigen::SimplicialLDLT and Eigen::SparseLU for the LDL^T and LU solvers
workload: Single-thread factorization on 34 SuiteSparse matrices (MultifrontalQR vs Eigen::SparseQR, 300 s cap for Eigen) and LDL^T of 3D Laplacians (lap3d 40^3, n=64000) vs Eigen::SimplicialLDLT.
claimed_speedup: MultifrontalQR 5x to 6900x faster than Eigen::SparseQR over the 34 matrices both finished, median 59x (README and doc/MultifrontalQR.md). SupernodalLDLT factor time 2640 ms vs Eigen::SimplicialLDLT 17724 ms on lap3d 40^3 (about 6.7x derived from page data; README says 6.5x) and 310 vs 1546 ms on lap3d 30^3 (about 5.0x derived).
compiler_and_flags: clang 22 -O3 stated for the SupernodalLDLT and parallel-scaling measurements; the QR table's page names no compiler
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5950X (16 cores) stated for the parallel scaling runs in doc/Parallelism.md; the QR and LDL^T tables name no CPU
tradeoffs: Header-only on top of Eigen with C++17; MPL-2.0; optional METIS, OpenMP, TBB and MKL PARDISO backends; SupernodalLU needs a symmetric pattern, LeftRightLU and PointBlockLU take any pattern.
caveats: Eigen::SparseQR is a weak baseline (slow, fill-heavy, wrong rank on several matrices), so the large ratios partly reflect that; no comparison with SuiteSparseQR, CHOLMOD or UMFPACK. Own benchmarks, best of 3, one machine, and CPU named only for the parallel runs. The repo's GitHub description says it was implemented with Claude Code, the repo is very new (its docs date measurements from 2026-08-22) and has 0 stars.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch 'github sparse LU direct solver "faster than SuperLU_DIST" open source' surfaced rhiestan/DirectLUSolvers; README and doc/*.md opened via raw.githubusercontent.com and WebFetch

name: apxchol (parallel approximate-Cholesky PCG for Laplacian and SDDM systems)
baseline: hypre BoomerAMG (CPU and GPU builds); AMGCL, RCHOL and ParAC are also in the comparison
workload: Setup plus solve time to 1e-8 true residual of the original system on 27 matrices (grids, interior-point matrices, SuiteSparse/SNAP graphs), one right-hand side, 72 threads on a GH200 node, median-total repetition after a warmup.
claimed_speedup: Derived from benchmarks/daint/results.csv (total time, CPU apxchol 'bg+tree' vs competitor): geometric-mean 5.7x faster than CPU BoomerAMG (median 4.6x, min 1.6x, max 123x, faster on all 26 matrices where both finished); 2.4x geometric mean vs CPU AMGCL (median 1.2x, faster on 21 of 27, slower on 6); 33x vs ParAC; GPU apxchol vs GPU BoomerAMG only 1.04x geometric mean (faster on 14 of 26).
compiler_and_flags: Clang 22.1.8 with libomp for CPU runs; GCC 14.3 as CUDA host compiler for GPU runs; CMake Release; exact optimisation flags not stated
hardware: NVIDIA GH200 node (72-core Grace CPU plus Hopper GPU), 72 threads
tradeoffs: Graph-Laplacian and SDDM systems only, not general SPD; approximate factor used as a PCG preconditioner; needs a C++23 compiler and Eigen (fetched if absent); CPU solve is memory-bound, so thread placement across NUMA domains matters (0.77 relative time at 32 threads over 4 domains vs 1.00 at 16 threads on one domain).
caveats: First-party benchmark with a strict measurement contract (true residual 1e-8, warmups, committed CSV with source hashes) but run on one GH200 node and recorded as a historical snapshot, not the current checkout; competitor adapters were written by the same authors. AMGCL is faster on 6 of 27 matrices and GPU apxchol is at parity with GPU BoomerAMG. BSD-4-Clause has the advertising clause; check OSI status before relying on 'copyable'. Neither SuiteSparse solvers, Eigen nor PETSc is in the timing table.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/cholesky listing led to AlgOptGroup/apxchol; README, benchmarks/README.md, benchmarks/daint/summary.md and results.csv opened via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: ALBUS (SIMD and load-balanced SpMV)
baseline: CSR5 (ICS'15); the paper abstract also names Intel MKL and merge-based SpMV (SC'16), and the README table lists CVR (CGO'18)
workload: SpMV in GFlops on 28 SuiteSparse matrices on a dual-socket Xeon Gold 6242 (README table); paper: 20 regular and 20 irregular matrices on a dual-socket Xeon E5-2670 v3.
claimed_speedup: README abstract (Future Generation Computer Systems 2021): average 1.59x / 1.32x / 1.48x (up to 2.53x / 2.22x / 2.31x) over CSR5 / Merge / MKL on regular matrices and 1.38x / 1.42x / 2.44x (up to 2.33x / 2.24x / 5.37x) on irregular matrices. README table: ALBUS above CSR5 on all 28 matrices (geometric mean 1.29x, range 1.02x to 2.71x, derived from page data) and above CVR on 25 of 28 (geometric mean 1.24x, derived); the MKL and Merge columns of that table are empty.
compiler_and_flags: icpc -xCORE-AVX2 -qopt-prefetch=3 -fopenmp -O3 (version not stated; g++ also supported)
hardware: Dual-socket Intel Xeon Gold 6242 (2 x 16 cores) for the README table; paper abstract: dual-socket Xeon E5-2670 v3
tradeoffs: Needs AVX2 and a one-time conversion/preprocessing step; Intel compiler by default; two variants (OpenMP and OpenMP+AVX2).
caveats: Benchmark by the authors. MKL and Merge numbers are only in the paper abstract quoted in the README, not in the table; preprocessing cost is not part of the table. The FGCS paper page was not opened.

name: cuBool (sparse Boolean linear algebra on CUDA)
baseline: SuiteSparse on CPU (README does not say which package; GraphBLAS likely)
workload: Boolean sparse matrix-matrix multiplication M*M and element-wise addition M+M^2 on 10 SuiteSparse graphs (62K to 2.2M rows), SpBench harness, operation time only with data already resident.
claimed_speedup: SpBench README table, time in ms, cuBool vs SuiteSparse for M*M: 23.2 vs 257.6 on amazon0312 (about 11x, derived from page data), 33.3 vs 369.5 on amazon-2008 (11x), 41.8 vs 673.3 on web-Google (16x), 18.1 vs 66.6 on roadNet-PA (3.7x), 1.9 vs 7.9 on wing (4.2x), 35.3 vs 90.9 on netherlands_osm (2.6x), 2.4 vs 3.1 on luxembourg_osm (1.3x); element-wise addition 11.4 vs 37.2 on amazon0312 (3.3x) and 24.8 vs 77.5 on web-Google (3.1x).
hardware: Intel Core i7-6700 3.40 GHz, 64 GB DDR4, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1070 8 GB, Ubuntu 20.04
tradeoffs: Boolean semiring only; needs an NVIDIA GPU (OpenCL sibling clBool/SPbLA exists); Python bindings (pycubool); GPU memory 91 to 241 MB in the table, while SuiteSparse used 22 MB on the smallest matrix.
caveats: GPU against CPU, which SpBench itself calls 'not entirely fair'; some compared libraries emulate Boolean operations with floats; SuiteSparse package, version and thread count not stated; cuSPARSE and clBool beat cuBool on some rows (for example luxembourg_osm and several addition rows). Benchmark is by the same project family; the 2021 GrAPL paper linked from the README was not opened. Evidence tier B because compiler version and optimisation flags are only given as 'GCC' and 'Release'.

name: spla (generalized sparse linear algebra with vendor-agnostic GPU acceleration)
workload: BFS, SSSP, PageRank and triangle counting on 10 to 13 SuiteSparse/SNAP/LAW graphs; spla on a GTX 1070 and on integrated GPUs against LAGraph on the host CPU, speedup chart.
claimed_speedup: Read by eye from the log-scale charts in the README (approximate, no numeric table): spla on GTX 1070 vs LAGraph, PageRank roughly 7x to 65x, triangle counting roughly 4x to 12x, SSSP roughly 1.4x to 23x, BFS roughly 0.7x to 3.7x. On integrated GPUs PageRank is up to about 11x (Intel HD 530) but BFS stays below 1x (about 0.1x to 0.8x) and triangle counting on the Ryzen iGPU is about 0.1x to 0.3x.

name: fast_matrix_market (parallel Matrix Market sparse matrix I/O)
baseline: C++ IOStreams (std::istream/ostream) and scanf-based Matrix Market loaders; for the Python bindings, scipy.io.mmread/mmwrite before SciPy 1.12
workload: Reading and writing Matrix Market sparse matrix files, thread-scaling plots on a laptop.
claimed_speedup: README: more than 1 GB/s read and write on a laptop, about 25x improvement over IOStreams; Python README shows read and write speedup plots over SciPy 1.10.0 (plots only, no numbers in text).
hardware: a laptop (model not stated; the companion parse-bench repo says an M1 MacBook Pro)
stars_or_usage: 91 stars; included as scipy.io.mmread and mmwrite from SciPy 1.12 per the README
tradeoffs: Needs C++17 (uses std::from_chars, falls back to fast_float and Dragonbox); ready-made bindings for GraphBLAS, Eigen, CXSparse, Blaze and Armadillo; supports all Matrix Market fields and the array format.

Benchmark methodology (compiler, flags, CPU) is not stated in the README. Python bindings are already merged into SciPy 1.12, so the Python speedup applies only to older SciPy.
